title: Film Workers' Body Asks PM Modi to Block Fawad Khan's Pakistani Netflix Series in India
excerpt: The All India Cine Workers Association wants Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo kept off Netflix India ahead of its December 4 global premiere, and a permanent law against Pakistani content on Indian platforms.
body:
• The All India Cine Workers Association (AICWA) has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi asking that the Pakistani series Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo not be streamed on Netflix in India.
  • The Urdu-language series, starring Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan, is Netflix's first Pakistan-themed original and is set for a global premiere on December 4, 2026.
  • AICWA's four demands include strict enforcement of the government's May 8, 2025 advisory against Pakistani-origin content and a permanent law with penalties covering TV, streaming and cinemas.
  • For viewers outside India: the demand concerns Netflix India only. The December 4 global premiere goes ahead as announced, so the series will be watchable on Netflix in the US and other countries regardless of New Delhi's decision.

The All India Cine Workers Association has written to Prime Minister Narendra Modi demanding that Netflix be stopped from releasing the Pakistani series Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo in India, ten days before the show's scheduled global premiere on December 4. The two-page letter, dated November 24, 2026 and signed by AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta, was also marked to Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and to Netflix India, and the association posted copies of it on its official X account on Tuesday.

"Terror Gets No Applause. Nation Comes First."

— All India Cine Workers Association, in its post announcing the letter

What the series is

Jo Bachay Hain Sang Samait Lo is an Urdu-language drama adapted from Farhat Ishtiaq's bestselling novel of the same name, and it is Netflix's first Pakistan-themed original series. The cast is led by Fawad Khan and Mahira Khan, alongside Hania Aamir and Sanam Saeed. Netflix recently unveiled the first-look poster and announced the December 4 global premiere. The title has also appeared in Netflix India's upcoming listings, but Netflix has not yet issued a statement clarifying whether the series will actually be available to viewers in India.

The four demands

AICWA's letter goes beyond this one series. The association has asked that the show not be streamed in India on December 4 or on any later date; that all OTT platforms strictly comply with the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting's advisory of May 8, 2025, which directed platforms operating in India to discontinue Pakistani-origin content; that the government introduce a permanent law, with penalties, restricting Pakistani content, artists and productions across television, streaming platforms and cinemas; and that Netflix India and other services publicly clarify their position on exhibiting Pakistani-origin content.

Why the body objects

In its letter, the association referred to the 2019 Pulwama attack and the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack in explaining its objection, and argued that making the series available to Indian audiences would go against the spirit of the May 2025 advisory. AICWA has opposed Pakistani artists working in India since Pulwama, and the government's advisory after Pahalgam extended the restrictions to streaming, covering Pakistani films, web series, songs and podcasts on platforms operating in India.

What happens next

The decision now sits with the government and Netflix. The December 4 date is a global premiere, and nothing in AICWA's letter affects the release outside India: subscribers in the United States, Canada, the UK and the Gulf will find the series on Netflix as scheduled. What remains open is the India listing. If the government backs the association's reading of its own advisory, Netflix India would be expected to drop or geo-block the title; if it does not act, the series could still appear for Indian subscribers on December 4. Netflix India's public clarification, which AICWA has demanded, would settle the question either way.
